newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Spain's CSI good for Arbed in longer term - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Spain's CSI good for Arbed in longer term - analysts.

text.p: Arbed's plan to buy 35 percent of Spain's Corporacion Siderurgica Integral (CSI) hold good, longer term prospects for the Luxembourg steel firm though synergies between the two were not obvious, analysts said.

"Arbed has the lowest share of coated products within its flat products (division) -- that's where the added value is and CSI is active in this business," said Olivier Heuschling, analyst at Belgium's Banque Bruxelles Lambert.
"It's very important to be near the final customer -- the car business (in Spain) is expanding and you have to be there to take advantage of it," he said.
Analysts say Arbed and CSI's combined 1996 crude steel production of 11.8 and 4.5 million tonnes respectively would rank them second in Europe after British Steel.
Spain's AIE state holding firm said on Tuesday it preferred Arbed over France's Usinor as a partner for CSI because it would increase productivity at the Spanish firm.

Under the terms of the deal, CSI will increase capital by 129.0 billion pesetas, with Arbed subscribing the whole issue for a 35 percent stake in the Spanish firm. CSI will then invest some 100 billion pesetas of that amount in stakes in Arbed group companies.
More details of the deal are still awaited, and it is not entirely clear exactly how Arbed will finance it.
Analysts saw no real cost cutting advantages for Arbed, especially as the plan means maintaining jobs at CSI.

Loic de Caters, analyst at Belgium's Generale Bank, said his initial reaction to the CSI deal was positive, though it did not make him more enthusiastic for Arbed shares which he already considered a "buy".
"Industrially speaking, (CSI is) modern, certainly not an ailing company...," he said.
Under the deal, CSI is taking a 9.5 percent stake in Arbed.
Caters did not expect this to dilute Arbed's earnings per share, because of the contribution to earnings that CSI would make.

Others said it was too soon to predict the effect of the deal on profitability for the Luxembourg company, which fell into a group loss of 1.2 billion francs in 1996 due to a sharp drop in steel prices.
One London steel analyst was less enthused by the deal.
"I'm a bit dubious. It looks like a dilution in what is an interesting recovery story going on in Arbed," he said.
"There is a problem with joint ventures as to what the benefits are and how you extract value from them in terms of cash."

While shares in Usinor suffered on the French bourse on Tuesday amid disappointment it was not picked to be CSI's partner, Arbed has risen 45 francs to 4,565 on the Brussels bourse in the past two days.

But dealers noted the stock was already being boosted along with shares in Belgian steel maker Cockerill by a bullish European Commission report on the outlook for the EU's steel industry, published last Friday.
